newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Powers offer more open market for telecom trade.
newsitem.headline: Powers offer more open market for telecom trade.

text.p: Telecom market liberalisation offers were made by a total of 68 countries in the World Trade Organisation negotiations on a global pact which ended in agreement at the weekend.
The following is a brief outline of the offers from the major powers, and from some of the key players in the developing countries.
THE UNITED STATES

The world leader, with just under 30 per cent of the global telecoms market of $600 billion in terms of revenue, committed itself to open markets for essentially all services for all market segments -- local, long-distance and international -- and unrestricted access to common carrier radio licences for operators that are indirectly foreign owned.
Its offer also covers satellite services and earth stations, international switching and other gateway facilities, cellular telephones and other mobile services.
Its few remaining limitations include no issue of radio licences to operators with more than 20 percent direct foreign ownership.
THE EUROPEAN UNION

The second-biggest global market, with a 28.3 per share of the total, it pledged its 15 members would complete liberalisation of basic telecom services, including satellite networks and services and all mobile and personal communications services and systems, by the year 2003.
Restrictions include a 20 percent foreign equity limit on radio-based services in France and a 25 percent limit on all services in Portugal.

Liberalisation is to be implemented from the beginning of 1998 in those EU states where it is not already under way, from December 1998 in Spain, by the year 2000 in Ireland and by the year 2003 in Portugal and Greece. JAPAN

The third market, with a 15.6 per cent share of global revenues, has agreed to remove long-standing foreign equity limits on most carriers and radio-based services, with the major exception of its two giant firms NTT and KDD which will retain a foreign equity ceiling of 20 per cent.
Otherwise, open access to outside firms and investors is committed in most markets for telecom services. AUSTRALIA
After the Big Three, the fourth global market with a 1.89 per cent share, it has pledged unrestricted competition in virtually all basic telecom services from July 1997.

It has also offered to end limits on the number of satellite service providers, currently set at two, and on suppliers of public mobile cellular telephones and facilities-based carriers, both currently set at three, also as of July 1997. CANADA

Number five, with 1.78 per cent of the world market, it came under heavy fire from the United States and criticism from the EU and other powers for insisting on limiting foreign ownership of facilities-based services to 20 percent direct and 46.7 per cent indirect.

Routing restrictions and foreign equity limits on many other services will be phased out by the year 2000, and restrictions on obtaining licences to land submarine cables will be removed as of October 1998.

The Teleglobe company's monopoly on overseas services will be eliminated and its foreign equity limits will be raised to the 46.7 per cent ceiling by October 1998. Telsat Canada's exclusive rights on satellite facilities and earth stations serving the U.S./Canada market will be eliminated as of April 2002.
BRAZIL

Number eight, and the biggest market among emerging economies, holds a 1.43 per cent share behind Switzerland and South Korea and has promised to end the state monopoly in the sector and offer improved commitment on public telecom services within one year of the passage of a new telecommunications law now in preparation.

It also commits to open markets for paging services and for the supply to closed user groups of all basic telecom services, including voice, and to phase out the 49 percent foreign equity limits on cellular telephony and satellite transport services as of July 1999.
SINGAPORE

Number 15, with only 0.42 per cent of the global market, it was nevertheless seen as a leader for other emerging economies. It commits to opening markets for mobile data, cellular telephony and trunked radio services and for paging services from April 2000.

It also pledged to provide for the domestic and international resale of public-switched capacity -- apart from the connection of leased lines to public network -- for most basic services, including voice and data. Foreign equity will be limited to 49 percent in most firms.
